reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Caused by Rickettsia conorii and transmitted by the brown dog tick (Rhipicephalus sanguineus), with dogs acting as an important reservoir and amplifier
Endemic around the Mediterranean basin, in southern Europe, Africa and parts of Asia, with a summer peak reflecting tick activity
After an incubation of about 5-7 days there is abrupt fever, headache and myalgia followed within a few days by a maculopapular rash
A black necrotic eschar at the bite site, the tache noire, is a highly suggestive sign and is often single; careful search of skin folds may reveal it
Unlike many exanthems the rash frequently involves the palms and soles and can become purpuric in severe disease
Doxycycline is the treatment of choice and should be given empirically on clinical suspicion rather than awaiting confirmatory serology

Most cases are self-limiting but a severe malignant form with vasculitic complications occurs, particularly in older patients, those with alcohol-related liver disease, diabetes or glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
reference.pathophysiology: Rickettsia conorii is an obligate intracellular bacterium inoculated during tick feeding that targets vascular endothelial cells. Local replication at the inoculation site produces the characteristic necrotic eschar (tache noire) through focal vasculitis and dermal necrosis, while dissemination causes a generalised small-vessel vasculitis analogous to other spotted fever rickettsioses. Endothelial injury increases vascular permeability and activates coagulation, producing the rash and, in severe cases, organ dysfunction affecting the brain, kidneys and lungs.
additionalDifferentials: Other spotted fever group rickettsioses including Rocky Mountain spotted fever
additionalInvestigations: Indirect immunofluorescence antibody serology on paired sera (confirmatory but often negative in the first week)
PCR of blood or of an eschar or skin biopsy
Full blood count looking for thrombocytopenia and leucopenia
redFlags: Confusion, meningism or focal neurology suggesting encephalitic involvement
Purpuric rash with hypotension indicating the malignant form
Acute kidney injury or respiratory compromise
Underlying immunosuppression, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency or chronic liver disease predisposing to severe illness
reference.prognosis: The majority of cases resolve fully with timely doxycycline, but the severe malignant form carries appreciable mortality, especially in older or comorbid patients, so early empirical treatment is important.
pitfalls: Overlooking the tache noire because it is painless and hidden in a skin fold, scalp or groin
Waiting for serological confirmation before starting doxycycline
Attributing the illness to a simple viral exanthem and missing palm and sole involvement
Failing to recognise host factors that predict the malignant form
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Empirical doxycycline, a tetracycline, started on clinical suspicion without waiting for serological confirmation
A macrolide such as azithromycin or clarithromycin as an alternative in mild disease or where tetracyclines are contraindicated
Supportive care with fluids and antipyretics
Monitor for the severe malignant form with neurological, renal and respiratory organ dysfunction, escalating to intensive care when needed
Advise tick-bite avoidance and control of the brown dog tick reservoir to prevent reinfection
Heightened vigilance and prompt treatment in older or comorbid patients, who are at greatest risk of severe disease
